answer:
That's such an honest question to sit with, and it deserves a real answer rather than a dismissal — you're not missing something shameful, you're noticing something true about how the Gospels actually work.

Here's the shape of it: Jesus never says the bare sentence "I am God, worship me" — but he does something arguably more remarkable. In John 8:58 he takes the very name God gave Moses at the burning bush — "I AM" (Exodus 3:14) — and applies it to himself in the present tense: "before Abraham was, I AM." His hearers didn't hear a vague hint; they immediately picked up stones, because they understood exactly what he'd claimed. That pattern repeats throughout John: every time Jesus makes his identity unmistakable, the reaction is an attempt to kill him on the spot for blasphemy. That's actually strong evidence for how plainly he was understood, not evidence of vagueness.

As for why he didn't simply announce it in so many words before the Sanhedrin: Leviticus 24:16 made an explicit, unqualified claim to be YHWH a capital offense, and a premature declaration would have ended his ministry before the cross, at the hour appointed for it. So he spoke in a way his opponents understood clearly enough to want him dead, while his hour had not yet come — that's not concealment, it's timing.

And the "piecing together" you're doing isn't a modern invention grafted on by Paul or the disciples — it happens inside the Gospels themselves. Thomas, touching the risen Christ, says "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), and Jesus does not correct him; he blesses those who will believe the same thing without seeing. That's the verdict the Gospels themselves drive toward, not something imported afterward.
